H8186B.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes shivering, trembling, physical fright in the face of evil. It is a spelling variant of a synonymous word (שַׁעֲרוּרָה). The family of words shares the idea of something that bristles, that causes one to recoil: in biblical Hebrew, this image of hair standing on end, of the body contracting before the abominable, is found.
H8186B.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible (two occurrences as a variant). In Jeremiah 18:13, the prophet uses it to describe Israel's apostasies, the people's infidelities to the Lord. In Hosea 6:10, it characterizes acts of prostitution and defilement that Ephraim engages in (a name for the Northern kingdom). In both cases, it is a term that accentuates prophetic judgment: it is not merely about sins, but about acts so repugnant that they provoke the horror of heaven itself. The context is always that of Israel's religious and moral infidelity.
H8186B.portee: This word reminds the reader that sin is never neutral: before God, there are no small acceptable transgressions. Certain acts, particularly those that violate the covenant and holiness of the Lord, provoke in God a legitimate repulsion. For the Christian, this invites a serious consideration of the gravity of moral evil and not to trivialize what is abominable in the eyes of the Lord.

sens: Man of the tribe of Benjamin, son of Azel and brother of several sons of King Saul
H8187.detail: Schearia is a Benjaminite mentioned twice in Chronicles, always as the son of Azel (1 Chronicles 8:38 and 9:44). He is one of the six sons of Azel, alongside his brothers Azrikam, Bocru, Ishmael, Obadiah, and Hanan. Azel himself was of the lineage of King Saul, placing Schearia in the royal Benjaminite line during the divided monarchy.
H8187.origine: The name Schearia means "esteemed by the Lord" or "valued by Jehovah," composed of Hebrew roots expressing esteem or value (שְׁעַר, estimation) and the divine name (יָה, Jehovah). This type of theophoric name, including the name of God, was common among families of ancient Israel, particularly in the royal lineage.
H8187.emploi: Schearia appears only twice in Scripture, both in the first book of Chronicles. The two passages (1 Chronicles 8:38 and 9:44) reproduce the same genealogy of the family of Azel, likely to establish the complete genealogical record of Saul's descendants during the divided monarchy. No action or particular event is attributed to him in the Bible.

sens: Priest serving in the temple during the reign of King David
H8188.detail: Séorim was a priest who served in the temple during the reign of King David. He was responsible for the fourth team (or "course") of priests tasked with serving in rotation before God (1 Chronicles 24:8). His name literally means "barley" in Hebrew, but here it designates a specific man, a member of the priestly tribe of Levi.
H8188.origine: The name Séorim comes from the Hebrew word śəʿōrâ which means "barley," the grain that the Hebrews commonly cultivated. It was a common practice in Israel to name a child after a plant or a product of the land. The exact significance of the link between this name and the function of this priest is not explained in the biblical text.
H8188.emploi: Séorim is mentioned only once in the entire Bible, in 1 Chronicles 24:8, in the list of the twenty-four courses of priests that David established to ensure the regular service of the temple. Each of these course leaders directed a group of priests who took turns for the sacrifices and maintenance of the sanctuary. Séorim was the head of the fourth team, which shows his importance in the organization of Davidic worship.

sens: City of Judah in the Shephelah region
H8189G.detail: 1. Schaaraïm is a city located in Judah, mentioned in the enumeration of the cities of the tribe (Joshua 15:36). The name literally means "double gate" in Hebrew, which likely refers to the main gates of this fortified city. It is a locality in the Shephelah, the region of coastal hills between the mountains of Judah and the Philistine plain.
H8189G.origine: The Hebrew name שַׁעֲרַיִם (shaârayim) is composed of שַׁעַר (shaâr, "gate") in the plural: literally "double gate" or "two gates." This formation suggests a fortified city with characteristic access gates, a common designation for cities in biblical times.
H8189G.emploi: Schaaraïm appears twice in the Bible. First, it is listed among the cities of Judah enumerated after the conquest (Joshua 15:36), alongside Adithaim, Gedera, and Gederothaim. Then, it is mentioned during the pursuit of the Philistines after David's victory over Goliath: the men of Israel pursued the fleeing enemies "as far as the way to Schaaraïm" toward Gath and Ekron (1 Samuel 17:52), indicating its strategic location on a route of escape toward Philistine territory.

sens: Fortified city of the tribe of Simeon in ancient Israel
H8189H.detail: Schaaraïm is a small city in the territory of Simeon mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:31. It is listed among the cities belonging to the descendants of Simeon up to the time of David.
H8189H.origine: The name Schaaraïm literally means "double gate" or "double portal" in Hebrew: sha-a-ra-yim, where "shaar" (שַׁעַר) denotes a gate or fortified portal, and the suffix "-ayim" indicates the dual (the pair, the double). This name likely reflects the defensive structure of the city, equipped with two main gates. In the Segond, this city is also called Sharuhen (שָׁרוּחֶן).
H8189H.emploi: Schaaraïm appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:31, where it is listed among the cities of the territory of Simeon. It is cited with other localities such as Beth-Marcaboth, Hazar-Susim, and Beth-Birei, in the context of the Simeonite possessions before the reign of David. This historical mention, without further detail, indicates that it was a sufficiently established settlement to be recorded in the registers of Israelite cities.

sens: Eunuch in the service of King Xerxes, responsible for overseeing the women of the second harem
H8190.detail: Schaaschgaz is an eunuch employed in the palace of the Persian King Xerxes. His role is to supervise the women who reside in the second house of the royal harem. It is through him that every woman destined for the king must spend a night before being called by the sovereign, as shown by his only mention in Esther 2:14, during the beauty contest that will lead to Esther's coronation.
H8190.origine: The name Schaaschgaz literally means "servant of beauty" in Persian (or Old Persian). This name reflects the function of this man within the palace administration: to oversee the beauty and appearance of the women in the harem, preparing and presenting them to the king according to royal protocols.
H8190.emploi: Schaaschgaz appears only once in the entire Bible, in Esther 2:14. He is mentioned in the context of the reforms of King Xerxes' harem after the dismissal of Queen Vashti. His role was administrative and honorific: he ensured that each woman destined for the king received appropriate care and went through the mandatory process before being presented to the sovereign.

sens: That which brings joy, happiness, what one loves above all
That which intensely pleases, that which rejoices the heart
That in which one finds satisfaction and contentment
H8191.detail:
1. The word designates that which provides deep and lasting joy — not a light or fleeting pleasure, but that which fills the heart with satisfaction. In the Psalms, particularly in Psalm 119, the one who prays says that God's precepts and law "are" his delights: this means that the Word of God becomes for him a source of true joy, more precious than anything. Example: "Your precepts are my delights; they are my counselors" (Psalms 119:24).

2. The word can also refer to the very object that causes this joy — the thing or person that one cherishes. In the Book of Proverbs, Wisdom says that she "delighted daily" in the presence of God: she was that in which God found his joy, his constant pleasure. This is an image of tenderness and intimacy (Proverbs 8:30).

3. Overall, the word expresses a state of deep contentment, a satisfaction of the heart — which contrasts with pain and anxiety. Even in distress, the one who finds delight in the law of God possesses a secret joy that sustains and preserves him (Psalms 119:92).
H8191.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to entertain oneself," "to play," "to find pleasure." It evokes the idea of play, amusement, recreation — that which in itself soothes and rejoices. The word is often used in the plural in Hebrew ("delights"), which reinforces the idea of a rich and multiple joy. It is a word that emphasizes the emotional and affective side of happiness, not its reason.
H8191.emploi: The word appears nine times in the Bible, mainly in the Psalms (five occurrences in Psalm 119 alone) and in Proverbs. In Psalm 119, which is a long hymn to the Law of God, the one who prays regularly returns to this theme: regardless of the circumstances, distress, anxiety, or misery, the Law and commandments of God remain his delights, his true joy. It is a motif of trust and endurance. In Proverbs (8:30-31), personified Wisdom describes herself as God's delights. In Jeremiah (31:20), God speaks of Ephraim as his beloved son, in whom his heart finds delight.
H8191.portee: This word reminds us that Christian joy is not superficial or dependent on circumstances, but can be anchored in the relationship with God and His Word. For the psalmist, making the divine Law his "delights" was not a morose obligation, but a source of true contentment and moral strength. This invites the reader to examine what truly brings them delight: what rejoices my heart? Do I seek my deep joy in the things of God, or elsewhere?

sens: To be stripped bare, made naked
To become denuded, without covering
To gradually lose what covers or protects it
H8192.detail: 1. The word first describes a physical action: to be scraped, swept away, or carried off by an external force. In Job 33:21, the flesh of the sick person "disappears" — it wears away and goes, leaving the bones visible, as if a ravaging illness were sweeping it away. 2. In a spatial sense, the word means to be stripped bare, emptied of all covering. In Isaiah 13:2, a banner is raised on a "naked" mountain, stripped of all vegetation or structure — an exposed place, without shelter. 3. By extension, the word evokes the idea of loss, of stripping away: what covered disappears, what concealed goes away, leaving the raw, the vulnerable.
H8192.origine: The Hebrew verb comes from a root that evokes the action of sweeping, scraping, or scouring. The niphal form (which is used here) indicates an action that happens to the subject: the subject does not sweep, but is swept away, stripped. The word always implies an external force — the wind, illness, wear — that gradually removes what covers.
H8192.emploi: The verb appears twice in the Hebrew Bible, in two distinct contexts. In Job 33:21, it describes the ravages of a serious illness: the flesh of the suffering man disappears, consumed by fever, while his bones become visible. In Isaiah 13:2, it qualifies a "naked" mountain, a bare summit, an ideal place for a banner that must be seen from afar. In both cases, the verb paints the image of loss, of stripping away, but applied to different realities: the human body here, geography there.
H8192.portee: This word reminds the reader of the fragility of the human body: illness can reduce it, wear it down, leave it exposed and vulnerable. For the believer, it is an invitation not to place trust in physical strength, but to turn to God alone in times of stripping and trial.

sens: Part of the human body that outlines the mouth
Language, speech, what comes out of the mouth
Edge, bank, border of an object or surface
Promise or commitment stated
H8193G.detail:
1. The lip is the fleshy part that surrounds the mouth: it is primarily the visible and fragile aspect of the human body. In Song of Solomon 4:3, the beloved's lips are compared to a scarlet thread, a beautiful poetic image.
2. The word also refers to the speech and language that comes from the mouth: what a person says reveals their heart. In Proverbs 10:19, "the multitude of words does not go without sin" shows that the lips are the instrument of sin through speech. In Proverbs 8:6, Wisdom says, "my lips open to teach what is right."
3. Lip can also mean the edge or bank of something: the rim of a cup, the bank of a river or sea. It is the image of the contour that limits a surface.
4. Finally, lip refers to spoken words as a commitment: in Numbers 30:7 and following, when someone "utters a vow from their lips," it is a solemn promise before God.
H8193G.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the idea of border and limit. The same root is found in connection with what borders, what encircles. In biblical Hebrew, "lip" is used from the Old Testament to refer both to the member of the body and, by extension, to the speech that comes from it. This transition from the concrete to the figurative is natural: what comes from our lips defines us.
H8193G.emploi: The word appears more than a hundred times in the Bible, especially in the Psalms and Proverbs, as well as in Job. Its most frequent and rich usage concerns speech: the quality of what we say, our promises, our lies, our gossip. In Exodus 6:12, Moses complains of not having "easy speech," meaning he is awkward in expression. Proverbs uses lip to describe foolish chatter (Proverbs 10:19), lying lips (Proverbs 12:22), lips of knowledge (Proverbs 15:7). The word also appears in the context of vows and oaths: when one "utters" something from their lips (Numbers 30), it is a solemn act before God. More rarely, it designates a physical edge.
H8193G.portee: This word reminds us of the immense power of speech. Our lips, small as they are, express what resides in our heart: they can bless or curse, encourage or destroy. The Bible warns us against the careless and deceitful use of speech, and urges us to be mindful of our promises, for what comes from our lips commits us before God. That is why Wisdom recommends weighing our words carefully.

sens: Part of the body that borders the mouth
Words, speech, what comes out of the mouth
Language, idiom, way of speaking specific to a people
Edge, bank, border of a surface or expanse
H8193H.detail:
1. The lip is primarily the part of the human body that closes the mouth (Proverbs 4:24: "Put away from you a deceitful mouth, and put perverse lips far from you"). It is what is seen, what can be closed or opened.
2. By natural extension, "lips" refer to what comes out of the mouth: the spoken words. The Bible speaks of wise lips (Proverbs 16:21: "the sweetness of the lips increases knowledge") or perverse lips (Proverbs 19:1) to talk about what a person says and which reveals their character.
3. A whole language, the way of speaking of a people is also called "lips" or a "lip": Isaiah 33:19 speaks of the "people of a strange language," literally "the people of an obscure lip," meaning whose language is not understood (Ezekiel 3:5-6: peoples "of foreign speech").
4. In a spatial sense, lips or lip refer to the edge, the bank, the shore of an expanse: the edge of a cup, of a sea, of a river — the visible limit where two worlds meet.
H8193H.origine: The Hebrew word (saphah) primarily designates the physical lip. The semantic shift to "speech" comes from the fact that the lip is the organ of speech, the visible starting point of discourse: what comes from the lips is what is said. The same word extends to "edge" or "bank" through a similar image: just as the lip borders the mouth, the bank borders the sea. The lips of a cup are its rim. This economy of vocabulary is typical of ancient language: one word designates the organ, its product (speech), and its figurative uses.
H8193H.emploi: The word appears 22 times in the Old Testament, very often in Proverbs (ten occurrences), which use it to speak of the quality of words: wise or foolish lips, sweet or perverse, sincere or deceitful. Proverbs 10:10 states that the fool's lips lead to his ruin, Proverbs 16:21 that the sweetness of the lips increases knowledge, Proverbs 20:19 that one should not disclose secrets with one who opens their lips too much. The sense of "language" is also found (Isaiah 33:19, Ezekiel 3:5-6, Zephaniah 3:9: "I will change the lips of the peoples," meaning their language). The spatial sense (edge, bank) is less frequent but clear. In 2 Kings 18:20, "empty words" literally translates to "words of lips," meaning hollow words, without substance.
H8193H.portee: This word reminds the reader that speech is embodied: it does not descend from heaven; it comes from our lips, it engages our body. Proverbs use it to teach that our words reveal our inner character ("The one who is foolish of lips runs to his ruin") and that they carry weight in life ("the sweetness of the lips increases knowledge"). For the Christian, it is an invitation to monitor what comes from their lips, knowing that our words shape our relationships and our reputation.

sens: Lip, edge of the mouth
Language, speech, tongue
Bank or shore of a body of water
Edge, border, or extremity of an object
Rim or raised border of a container
H8193I.detail:
1. The edge of the mouth, the lip as part of the body; this is the most concrete and basic meaning of the word.
2. The tongue, the language, the speech — because it comes from the mouth and its lips: it is a natural image to designate what we speak and the way we communicate.
3. The bank or shore of a river, stream, or sea — the place where water meets land (for example, Deuteronomy 4:48: "from Aroer, which is by the edge of the river Arnon").
4. The edge, the border, the contour of an object, particularly of a fabric or garment (Exodus 26:4: "you shall make blue cords on the edge of the curtain"), or the opening that must be finished carefully.
5. The rim of a container, the raised edge of a basin or a bronze sea — what marks its limit and can contain what it holds (1 Kings 7:24: "gourds surrounded it below its edge").
H8193I.origine: The Hebrew word saphaḥ (שָׂפָה) comes from a root that primarily evokes the lip and the mouth, and naturally expands to anything that is an extremity, edge, or limit of a surface. The image of the lip — this line that delineates the mouth — has served as a model to describe any visible border: the edge of a garment, of an object, of a body of water. It is a very concrete word, rooted in the observation of the body and things.
H8193I.emploi: This word appears about 20 times in the Old Testament, especially in architectural and geographical descriptions. It is frequently found in the books of the Law (Exodus, Deuteronomy) to describe the finishes of priestly garments and elements of the tabernacle — the borders of curtains, the rims of breastplates, the openings of tunics (Exodus 26:4, Exodus 28:32, Exodus 39:19). It is also found in geographical descriptions of conquered lands, particularly to mark the waterways that delineate territories (Deuteronomy 4:48, Joshua 13:16). Finally, it is used to describe the rims of the large bronze basins of the temple (1 Kings 7:24, 2 Chronicles 4:2). In all cases, it designates a limit, a precise and visible extremity.
H8193I.portee: This word reminds the reader that God is attentive to detail — He does not disdain to prescribe how to finish a embroidery or a garment, both for beauty and durability. For those who meditate on these texts, it is an invitation to awareness: God sees to the edges, to the borders of what we do. It is also a humble and earthly word that brings faith back to the everyday: no mysterious poetry, but seams, shores, concrete objects that separate and delimit.

sens: Coast of a sea or body of water
Bank or shore of a river
Border, edge, or limit of something
Lip or edge of a container
H8193J.detail:
1. The edge of a sea or lake: the coastal area where water meets land. In Genesis 22:17, Abraham receives the promise that his descendants will be "like the sand that is on the edge of the sea" — an image of countless multitude that emphasizes vastness.

2. The bank or shore of a river: the land along a watercourse. Pharaoh "stood on the edge of the river" (Genesis 41:17), a classic image of power and observation in ancient Egypt, as the Nile was vital.

3. The border, ridge, or rim of an object: the outline that limits something. Ezekiel 47:6-7 speaks of trees at the "edge" of the miraculous river, marking the boundary of the irrigated area.

4. The lip or rim of a container, cup, or vase: the upper edge of a receptacle. Although attested in usage, this meaning is less frequent in the provided texts.
H8193J.origine: The Hebrew word שָׂפָה (saphah) comes from a root meaning "to border" or "to delimit." The concrete meaning of "lip" (the border of the face) is the oldest; from there derives the figurative meaning of "edge" or "border" of anything (water, object, territory). This is why the same word designates the lip of the body and the shore of the sea — both are boundaries, visible limits.
H8193J.emploi: The word appears about 17 times in the provided texts, especially in historical and prophetic narratives. It often refers to the edge of the sea or the Nile in Egyptian contexts (Pharaoh, Joseph, Exodus) and Eastern contexts, particularly to express multitudes: "like the sand of the edge of the sea" becomes a biblical formula for uncountability (Genesis 22:17, Joshua 11:4, 1 Samuel 13:5). The word is also used for the banks of ordinary rivers (Exodus 7:15) and, in the prophet Ezekiel, for the shores of the eschatological river that flows from the temple (Ezekiel 47:6-7).
H8193J.portee: This word reminds us that God controls boundaries and limits — both earthly and spiritual. The phrase "like the sand of the edge of the sea" expresses the infinity of God's promise to Abraham: not a measured or restricted blessing, but an abundance that exceeds human calculation. For the believer, the edge also symbolizes what separates two worlds or two realities (the dry and the wet, the known and the unknown), inviting us to see in God the one who creates order and sets boundaries.

sens: The organ in the mouth that allows for speech
The language spoken, the way to communicate through speech
The voice, what is heard when someone speaks
H8193K.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to the body part — the tongue we have in our mouth that allows us to articulate sounds. This is the most physical and concrete meaning.
2. By natural extension, the word comes to designate language itself, that is, the tongue spoken, the system of communication specific to a people. This is the dominant meaning in the provided biblical usages: at Babel, God "confused the language of all the earth" (Genesis 11:9), which means He created different languages so that men would no longer understand each other.
3. The word can also refer to the voice or what is heard: in Psalm 81:6, the psalmist says, "I hear a voice that is unknown to me," where the Hebrew word refers to the oral, to what comes out of someone's mouth.
H8193K.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of something pointed or protruding — the tongue that comes out of the mouth. The Hebrew word initially designated this physical organ, then the language it produces. This progression from the concrete to the figurative is very common in Hebrew: from the part of the body to the function or result of the function.
H8193K.emploi: The word appears six times in the cited passages, concentrated around the Babel narrative in Genesis 11, where it is central: before the confusion, all men spoke "one language" (11:1), a "same language" (11:6); then God confuses their "language" (11:7, 11:9), which creates barriers between peoples. Beyond Babel, Isaiah 19:18 announces that certain cities of Egypt "will speak the language of Canaan," imagery of a return to unity or alignment with the people of God. In Psalm 81:6, the word takes on the coloration of "voice" in translation. The meaning remains always linked to human communication, to what unites or divides peoples.
H8193K.portee: This word reminds us that language is a gift from God — and a responsibility. The confusion of languages at Babel shows that God controls the speech of men and uses it to judge pride and scatter corrupted unity. For the believer today, it is an invitation to use one's tongue wisely, knowing that it comes from God and has the power to build or destroy.

sens: Dairy product obtained by coagulating milk from cows or other animals
Preserved food, rich in nutrients, valued in ancient Near Eastern diets
H8194.detail:
1. The word designates cheese, this dairy product obtained by allowing milk to coagulate and transform. It is a solid food, unlike fresh milk, making it easy to transport and preserve for long periods — particularly useful in a warm climate. In 2 Samuel 17:29, inhabitants bring to David and his companions "cow's cheese" among other provisions, recognizing its nutritional value for men weakened by hunger and fatigue.
2. Cheese is a symbol of generosity and concrete help. The people who bring it show compassion towards David and his people in the wilderness: cheese, rich in fat and protein, restores strength after exertion.
H8194.origine: The Hebrew word שְׁפוֹת (shephot) specifically designates cheese or thick cream. Its root evokes the idea of transforming milk through a natural process. It is a concrete and ancient vocabulary, rooted in the pastoral life of the Near East, where cheese-making was a daily practice of shepherds and household women.
H8194.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in 2 Samuel 17:29. David, fleeing with his men, receives from generous people food aid that includes honey, cream, sheep, and cow's cheese. This unique usage illustrates the context of survival in the wilderness and the solidarity towards those suffering from hunger and exhaustion.
H8194.portee: This verse reminds us that practical and concrete help — feeding the hungry, relieving the suffering — is an expression of love for one's neighbor. The people who bring cheese to David act out of compassion in the face of misery, thus embodying the generosity that God values.

sens: Son of an Edomite, member of the genealogy of Esau
H8195.detail: 1. Schepho is a man's name that appears in the genealogical lists of the clan of Esau in Edom. He is the son of Shobal, himself the son of Seir, and the brother of Alvan, Manahath, Ebal, and Onam. These genealogies document the descendants of the peoples who inhabited the territory before the settlement of Israel.
H8195.origine: The name Schepho literally means "bold" or "daring," evoking a quality of courage or strength. It bears the mark of Edomite proper names, preserved in the Bible to document the families that lived in Edom, the southern region of the Dead Sea, territory of the descendants of Esau, the brother of Israel.
H8195.emploi: Schepho is mentioned only twice in the Bible: in Genesis 36:23 and in 1 Chronicles 1:40. These two passages present the same genealogy, that of Shobal son of Seir, where Schepho appears among his five sons. The name appears under two slightly different spellings: "Schepho" in Genesis and "Schephi" in 1 Chronicles. These genealogical lists serve to establish the ancient history of the peoples of the Near East contemporary with Abraham and Isaac.

sens: act of judging, pronouncing a condemnation
punishment, penalty inflicted
H8196.detail:
1. Judgment is primarily the act of judging, the verdict that is pronounced. It is the exercise of justice: evaluating, deciding what is right or wrong. In 2 Chronicles 20:9, King Jehoshaphat lists the calamities that could strike the people: "the sword, judgment, plague, or famine." Judgment is mentioned as a calamity among others — the sword of the warrior, disease, famine — meaning a trial that God may send as punishment.
2. Judgment also becomes the punishment itself, the result of the judgment pronounced. In Ezekiel 23:10, the prophet describes a woman who "has been renowned among women, after the judgments exercised upon her": these judgments are not trials, but punishments, acts of vengeance and destruction that enemies executed against her.
H8196.origine: The Hebrew word sheṕot comes from the root shāpaṭ ("to judge, govern"). This root originally evokes the idea of establishing order, resolving a dispute, rendering justice. It also gave rise to the title of "judge" (shôpēt) — a figure who, in the Old Testament, governed Israel by administering justice. Thus, judgment is the act of judges, their specific work: weighing the facts and pronouncing the sentence.
H8196.emploi: The word sheṕot appears twice in the Bible in this precise sense. In 2 Chronicles 20:9, it is found in a prayer of King Jehoshaphat: judgment is listed as a possible plague, a calamity sent by God. In Ezekiel 23:10, the prophet uses it to refer not to an act of judging, but to the concrete punishments — the "judgments exercised" — that enemies inflicted on a woman. The word thus oscillates between the trial (the act of judging) and its consequence (the punishment).
H8196.portee: Understanding that judgment is not an abstraction: it is a real act that produces effects. The Bible reminds us that God judges — He is not indifferent — but also that judging is serious. Judgment can be a grace (establishing justice) or a calamity (suffering punishment). For the believer, this is a reason for respectful fear of God and trust in His justice.

sens: Man of the tribe of Benjamin, son of Bela and grandson of Benjamin
H8197A.detail: Schupham is a man of the tribe of Benjamin, mentioned in the genealogical lists of the Old Testament. He appears as one of the descendants of Benjamin during the census of the people in the wilderness (Numbers 26:39). His descendants form the family of the Schuphamites, listed among the families of Benjamin on that occasion. He is also referred to as Shupham or Shephuphan in other biblical passages (1 Chronicles 8:5), and his name may also refer to Muppim according to some lists.
H8197A.origine: The name Schupham comes from the Hebrew שְׁפוּפָם. It literally means "serpent" according to tradition. It is a name given to a direct descendant of Benjamin, the son of Jacob, and it appears in the genealogies tracing the families of the tribes of Israel.
H8197A.emploi: Schupham is mentioned only once in the Segond 1910, in chapter 26 of Numbers, during the second census of the Israelites in the wilderness, after forty years of wandering from Egypt. On this occasion, the families descending from the sons of Benjamin are enumerated. The family of Schupham, called the Schuphamites, is listed alongside other Benjaminite families such as that of Hupham (the Huphamites). This appearance in the genealogical records confirms the importance of these families in the formation of the tribe of Benjamin at the time of settling in Canaan.

sens: Son of Benjamin and of the tribe of Israel
H8197B.detail: Schephuphan is a man of the tribe of Benjamin, mentioned in the genealogy of the descendants of Benjamin. His name appears in 1 Chronicles 8:5 in the list of the sons of Bela, himself a son of Benjamin. He is an ancestor of the Benjamites living during the time of Egypt and the wilderness.
H8197B.origine: The name Schephuphan (in Hebrew Schephuphan) literally means "serpent." It is a compound name evoking the image of the reptile, although the precise reason for this symbolic name eludes us. The same man is also called Shupham in Numbers 26:39, and his descendants form the clan of the Schephuphanites.
H8197B.emploi: Schephuphan is mentioned only once in the Segond 1910, in 1 Chronicles 8:5, in the genealogy of the sons of Bela, son of Benjamin. He belongs to the first generation of Israelites, the one that went down to Egypt. He appears only once in this genealogical passage, without any particular account regarding his life or actions.

sens: Woman of servile condition belonging to a master or mistress
Female slave, notably a captive of war or acquired by purchase
Person who voluntarily lowers herself and speaks with humility, out of respect or politeness
H8198.detail:
1. A maidservant is a woman who is enslaved, often acquired with the master's goods. She can be the personal property of a mistress, like Hagar whom Sarah owned (Genesis 16:1). She performs domestic tasks and her status is clearly inferior to that of free men and women. Genesis 12:16 shows that Pharaoh gave Abram maidservants among his gifts, just as one gives livestock or movable goods.
2. A slave in the Bible can be a prisoner of war or sold into slavery (Deuteronomy 28:68 mentions this threat). Leviticus 19:20 deals with a maidservant betrothed to another, showing that she does not have full authority over herself. She has few legal rights and can be punished without being put to death.
3. The word also designates, by humility and respect, one who speaks of herself in this way. The Samaritan woman addresses David saying "your maidservant" (2 Samuel 14:6-15) to present her case to him with deference, even though she is free. It is a polite formula towards the one being addressed, expressing a voluntary and respectful submission.
H8198.origine: The Hebrew word shiph'hah comes from a root that evokes lowering, subjugation. The feminine form emphasizes the particular condition of women in antiquity: they are often reduced to a state of total dependence. The word first designates a concrete social reality of the ancient Near East, where servitude was common and accepted. It has also taken on a nuance of modesty or deference when a free woman applied it to herself in speaking to a superior.
H8198.emploi: The word appears 58 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in the accounts of Genesis and the historical books. In Genesis, it designates the maidservants owned by the patriarchs: Sarah had Hagar (16:1-6), Jacob had maidservants given by his mothers and fathers-in-law (29:24, 29:29), and Leah and Rachel gave them to Jacob as concubines to bear children (30:4-12). The material sense of "maidservant" remains constant in Exodus, Leviticus, and Deuteronomy, where it appears in the laws regarding servitude. But the word also takes on a figurative sense when a free woman speaks of herself: the woman of Tekoa addresses David saying "your maidservant" (2 Samuel 14:6-19), expressing her reverence towards the king. The Psalms (123:2) use it to evoke the spiritual attitude of the believer towards God. The word remains a key element in the biblical vision of the master-servant relationship and humility.
H8198.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader of the concrete condition of women in antiquity and how God, in His Law, regulated servitude rather than outright prohibiting it. It also sheds light on how the Bible uses the image of the maidservant to express humility and deference towards God and those who are above us: calling oneself "maidservant" was to acknowledge one's place and dependence. This voluntary humility is one of the attitudes that the Bible values.

sens: Exercise the authority of a judge: render a sentence after examining a case
Govern a people, administer them, take care of them
Take sides for someone, defend them, vindicate them
Blame, condemn, and punish one who has acted wrongly
Discern between good and evil, settle a dispute
H8199.detail:
1. To judge is primarily to fulfill the role of a judge: to examine a case, listen to both parties, and render a fair judgment. Moses "judges" difficult cases in Exodus 18:16, and Deborah "was a judge in Israel" (Judges 4:4) — she had the authority to settle the people's disputes.

2. However, the word also means to govern and lead a people. The judges of Israel after Joshua were not just magistrates: they guided the entire nation, protected it, and organized it. This aspect dominates the book of Judges.

3. To judge can also mean "to defend someone," to vindicate them, to restore their rights. When the Lord brings "justice" to David by delivering him (2 Samuel 18:31), He justifies him before his accusers.

4. Conversely, to judge means to condemn and punish: the judge who identifies guilt must also impose the penalty. God "judges" crimes, corruption, sin — He identifies and punishes them.

5. Finally, to judge is to discern, to decide between two opposing positions. Abram asks God to be a "judge" between him and Sarai (Genesis 16:5): it is up to Him to decide who is right.
H8199.origine: The root שׁפט (sh-p-t) was already ancient in Hebrew and in the neighboring Aramaic. It evokes the idea of cutting, separating, rendering a verdict by distinguishing the just from the unjust. The word is related to terms of the same family meaning "judgment" (mishpat) and "judge" (shophet) — very common words in biblical Hebrew. The basic image is that of a judge who steps down from his place, confronts the parties, and pronounces the truth.
H8199.emploi: The verb "to judge" appears more than 180 times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in the historical books (Judges, Samuel, Kings) and legislative texts (Exodus, Deuteronomy). It is a fundamental word for describing authority in Israel: civil magistrates judge disputes (Exodus 18:13-26, Deuteronomy 16:18), kings judge the people (2 Samuel 15:4, 1 Kings 3:9), and even the prophets remind that God judges (Psalms 7:12, Ezekiel 20:4). The meaning naturally shifts between rendering a judicial verdict, governing, defending the oppressed, and punishing evil. In the Psalms and Proverbs, it is often God who judges: He sees all, judges justly, and condemns iniquity. Proverbs 31:9 calls on the magistrate: "Judge with justice, and defend the needy."
H8199.portee: This word shows the reader that justice is not an abstraction, but a concrete action: someone must judge. For the Christian faith, it reveals that God Himself judges fairly what we do and think — a truth that is both fearsome and reassuring. It also challenges us regarding our responsibility to administer justice to the weak and oppressed: we are called to reflect God's wise and just judgment. Finally, it sheds light on the role of Jesus as the eschatological judge: He is the one who, on the last day, will judge the living and the dead.
